a_raw: {"translation":"Target defines, but does not prove, the following proposition. For every input type X, every output type Y, and every S1 system N on those types, there exists an S1 system N' on the same types satisfying all three conditions: (1) N' has exactly one index (not necessarily just one possible state at that index). (2) For every two distinct indices m and n of N', it is not the case that there is both a nonempty directed dependency path from m to n and one from n to m. An edge from i to j means that there exist two state assignments agreeing everywhere except possibly at i, and an input on which the updates at j from those assignments differ. The assignments need not be reachable from the initial assignment. Condition (2) is vacuous with just one index and does not forbid a self-loop. (3) For every finite list of inputs from X, including the empty list and with no length bound, N' and N give equal outputs: each starts from its own initial assignment, updates on the inputs from left to right, and applies its own readout to the final assignment. The same N' must work for all lists; agreement of internal states is not required."}
translation: Target defines, but does not prove, the following proposition. For every input type X, every output type Y, and every S1 system N on those types, there exists an S1 system N' on the same types satisfying all three conditions: (1) N' has exactly one index (not necessarily just one possible state at that index). (2) For every two distinct indices m and n of N', it is not the case that there is both a nonempty directed dependency path from m to n and one from n to m. An edge from i to j means that there exist two state assignments agreeing everywhere except possibly at i, and an input on which the updates at j from those assignments differ. The assignments need not be reachable from the initial assignment. Condition (2) is vacuous with just one index and does not forbid a self-loop. (3) For every finite list of inputs from X, including the empty list and with no length bound, N' and N give equal outputs: each starts from its own initial assignment, updates on the inputs from left to right, and applies its own readout to the final assignment. The same N' must work for all lists; agreement of internal states is not required.

divergences.description: The singleton conclusion needs more than permission for a unit to have memory. Lean allows one unit to store the entire joint state of N and apply its entire transition function. The passage permits memory in flip-flops but does not say that an arbitrary automaton counts as one unit. A single binary flip-flop, for example, cannot realize a machine with three behaviourally distinguishable states.

The passage concerns finite-state automata. Lean requires only the set of unit indices to be finite; even a one-unit system can have infinitely many states. The target thus quantifies over systems outside the scope of the passage.

judgement.summary: Lean accurately states the proposed degenerate observation under its permissive definition of a unit: one twin works for every finite input history, and feedback between distinct units is vacuously absent. This is an independent observation about how units are counted, not a consequence of the passage’s use of memoryful flip-flops.
